name: Inbred-line hybrid maize breeding, United States
summary: Maize seed made each season by crossing inbred lines, restoring vigour and raising yield; George Shull published the method in 1908 and seed was sold from 1924.
description: George Harrison Shull, at Cold Spring Harbor, published in 1908 that crossing inbred maize lines gave vigorous, uniform, high-yielding hybrids, and in 1909 set out the breeding procedure. D. F. Jones's four-way (double-cross) hybrids, published in 1918, overcame the poor seed yield of inbred lines. Henry A. Wallace sold hybrid seed in 1924, and in Iowa hybrids went from under 10% of the maize crop in 1935 to well over 90% four years later.

impact.note: Hybrid maize took over the United States crop by the 1950s and then maize growing on several continents (reach 2), reorganised growing around seed bought new each year for a large yield gain (depth 2), and founded heterosis breeding and the commercial seed industry, later extended to other crops (generativity 2).

unresolved.note: Whether Wallace's 1924 sale was the first commercial hybrid seed: Crow says so, citing Crabb (1947), but a Connecticut-grown double cross is often said to have been sold in 1921. A second source is needed.

Where Jones worked (the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station) and the 1917 cross and 1918 field trial of the double cross are not stated on the cited page; the event is placed only in the United States.
The founding of Wallace's Hi-Bred Seed Corn Company in 1926 was removed from the description because it is not in the cited source; it needs a proper source.
East's Connecticut work and Shull's 1909 paper on the breeding procedure were not researched from primary sources.

research.note: Crow writes that Shull's 1908 paper 'marked the beginning of the exploitation of heterosis in plant breeding'; E. M. East, working on inbreeding at the same time, did not see the value of crossing inbred lines until he heard Shull's report in January 1908.
